Ithaca|United States of America.f: The city takes its name from the Greek island of Ithaca, home of Odysseus in Homer's Odyssey.

Lancaster|United States of America.f: During the American Revolution, Lancaster served for one day as the temporary capital of the United States.

Aberdeen (SD)|United States of America.f: Aberdeen was named after Aberdeen, Scotland, the birthplace of the Milwaukee Road railroad president who chose its name.

Pierre|United States of America.f: Pierre is the second-least populous U.S. state capital, ahead of only Montpelier, Vermont.

Dodge City|United States of America.f: Dodge City was staked out in 1872 on the 100th meridian, at the western edge of the Fort Dodge reservation.

Watertown (SD)|United States of America.f: Watertown was named after Watertown, New York, hometown of two founders, and was originally planned to be called Kampeska.

Williamsport|United States of America.f: Williamsport is the birthplace of Little League Baseball, and nearby South Williamsport hosts the Little League World Series.

Silver City|United States of America.f: In 1875 Sheriff Harvey Whitehill became the first lawman to arrest Billy the Kid, twice, for theft in Silver City.

Charlottesville|United States of America.f: Jefferson's Monticello and his University of Virginia Academical Village near the city are both UNESCO World Heritage Sites.

Rhinelander|United States of America.f: Rhinelander is home to the hodag, a folkloric green and white creature said to stalk the local woods.

Roanoke|United States of America.f: After the railroad picked Big Lick as its HQ in 1882, the town's population grew 22 times in the 1880s as it became Roanoke.

Hibbing|United States of America.f: The edge of town holds the Hull-Rust-Mahoning Open Pit Iron Mine, the world's largest open-pit iron mine.

Beaumont|United States of America.f: The 1901 Spindletop gusher showed a huge oil field lay under Beaumont and turned the area into a major refining hub.

Beckley|United States of America.f: Beckley is named for John James Beckley, the first Librarian of Congress, and was founded by his son Alfred.

Gustavus|United States of America.f: Gustavus is surrounded on three sides by Glacier Bay National Park and was once called Strawberry Point.

Charleston (WV)|United States of America.f: When Charleston was incorporated in 1794, its trustees included Daniel Boone.

State College|United States of America.f: Beaver Stadium, home of Penn State football, is the second-largest stadium in the Western Hemisphere.

Homer|United States of America.f: Homer is nicknamed the Halibut Fishing Capital of the World and sits at the end of a 4.5 mile gravel bar, the Homer Spit.

Bellingham|United States of America.f: Bellingham is the northernmost city with more than 90,000 people in the contiguous United States.

Muscle Shoals|United States of America.f: Aretha Franklin, Wilson Pickett and Percy Sledge recorded at Muscle Shoals' FAME Studios, founded by Rick Hall.

Texarkana|United States of America.f: Texarkana's federal courthouse sits on the Arkansas-Texas line and is the only federal office building to straddle a state line.

Albany (GA)|United States of America.f: The Creek people called the Albany site Thronateeska, their word for flint, found in beds near the Flint River.

El Dorado|United States of America.f: El Dorado's Busey No. 1 well started a 1921 oil boom that earned it the nickname Arkansas' Original Boomtown.

West Lafayette|United States of America.f: West Lafayette is the most densely populated city in Indiana and home to Purdue University.

Hot Springs|United States of America.f: The center of Hot Springs is the oldest federal reserve in the United States, now Hot Springs National Park.

Saranac Lake|United States of America.f: Dr. Edward Trudeau came to Saranac Lake in 1876 to treat his tuberculosis, and the village became a TB cure center.

White Plains|United States of America.f: Early traders called it the White Plains, either for white balsam said to cover it or mist over the swamps.

Fort Dodge|United States of America.f: The gypsum used to make the Cardiff Giant hoax of the late 19th century was mined at Fort Dodge.

Walla Walla|United States of America.f: Walla Walla is derived from a Nez Perce word for place of many waters, and its Italian growers developed the sweet onion.

Pellston|United States of America.f: The University of Michigan runs a biological station on nearby Douglas Lake, just outside the village of Pellston.

Lewiston|United States of America.f: Lewiston was the first capital of Idaho Territory and its port is the farthest inland port linked to the Pacific Ocean.

Thief River Falls|United States of Ameri.f: The name loosely translates the Ojibwe Stolen-land river, after Dakota who secretly camped on the river and were routed.

Hattiesburg|United States of America.f: Hattiesburg was named for Hattie, wife of founder William Hardy, and earned the nickname Hub City from its railroads.

Kalamazoo|United States of America.f: The city was originally called Bronson and was renamed Kalamazoo in 1836 after the river, whose name's meaning is disputed.

Dubuque|United States of America.f: Settled in 1788, Dubuque is the oldest city in Iowa and was named for French-Canadian lead miner Julien Dubuque.

Florence|United States of America.f: Railroad president General William Harllee built his home at the junction and named it Florence after his daughter.

Iron Mountain|United States of America.f: Iron Mountain sits next to the Pine Mountain Jump, one of the largest artificial ski jumps in the world.

Joplin|United States of America.f: In 1933 Bonnie and Clyde spent some weeks in Joplin, and fled after a shootout that killed two lawmen.

Jamestown (ND)|United States of America.f: Jamestown has the World's Largest Buffalo, a 26 foot tall sculpture of an American bison.

Houghton|United States of America.f: Houghton is the largest city in Michigan's Copper Country, where Cornish and Finnish immigrants came to work the copper mines.
